response.query: How can we quantify and correct measurement error from transformer NLP proxies (validation subsamples, SIMEX, latent‑variable measurement models)?
response.answer: Measurement error in transformer NLP proxies can be quantified and corrected using latent variable models and the SIMEX method. Latent variable models explicitly account for measurement error, while SIMEX simulates datasets to correct for it. Both methods improve model accuracy.

results.content: Two measurement models are generally used to represent latent variables: the reflective and the formative model. Latent variable models, including confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) and structural equation modeling (SEM), are statistical approaches in which multiple observed indicators are obtained in order to assess a desired latent construct (Brown, 2006; Kline, 2010). Muthén and Muthén’s (2002) simulation approach to statistical power for latent variables is highly recommended, as it encourages the researcher to explore *a priori* the effect of different expected parameter estimates on the power and precision of the overall statistical model. We have emphasized the crucial role of measurement error in preceding sections, and a significant advantage of latent variable methods over traditional analyses is their ability to explicitly model measurement error using multiple observed indicators of a variable. Within SEM, measurement models—the portion of the model relating latent variables to observed or manifest indicators—typically include multiple indicators of each construct. Relative to other latent variable models, the hallmark of an LDS model is the specification of a second-order latent variable that represents change between the first and second time points of assessment. However, these are not the only latent variable models of potential relevance for psychophysiological research. #### Extensions of latent variable models. Besides the crucial advantage of correcting for measurement error, the specification of latent variable models allows for important extensions that have promise for advancing developmental theory. Overall, latent variable models are under-utilized in research on psychophysiological reactivity. In particular, their ability to model measurement error and thereby account for unreliability in assessments is a crucial advantage: our review of psychometric issues has highlighted how unreliability can obscure the correct interpretation of observed DSs and RSs, and latent variable methods mitigate this serious problem. For example, adding an outcome variable to the LDS model allows for testing of a latent mediating pathway from baseline through reactivity to the outcome. In other words, after modeling estimation, each latent variable should be appropriately renamed by properly estimating results, especially by looking at those observed variables with statistically significant and larger standardized parameter values.

results.title: SIMULATION EXTRAPOLATION METHOD FOR MEASUREMENT ERROR: A REVIEW - PMC
results.content: SIMEX method involves simulating several pseudo-datasets (the number of datasets simulated is denoted by B) at each level of inflation of measurement error variance λ, followed by estimation of the coefficients of covariate *W* at each level of variance inflation. If we let *Y, X, W, Z* be the response variable, true covariate, naive covariate (observed version of *X*) and another correctly measured covariate, respectively, the estimator is then considered as a function of *(Y, X, Z).* The underlying assumption for the SIMEX procedure is that measurement error variance in *X* is either known or can be estimated from data. Carroll et al., (1996) investigated the asymptotic distribution of the SIMEX estimator and also demonstrated a technique for the estimation of asymptotic standard errors for the SIMEX estimator, when the covariate *W* is subject to additive measurement error in the context of a generalized linear model. The method used to correct for the effect of measurement error in *W,* on score function estimation bears similarity to the SIMEX method in that Monte Carlo datasets are generated at a preset value of rather than being extrapolated to this value. Simulations of non-parametric regression using a sample size of 500 and specifying Laplace distribution of measurement error revealed that the SIMEX method performed well in terms of minimizing ISE along with the data driven local linear method of Delaigle, Fan, and Carroll (2008), with both outperforming the naïve estimator. Simulation studies using a Weibull AFT model (time is assumed to follow Weibull distribution) showed that the sensitivity of the SIMEX method to the approximate nature of the extrapolation function increased with increasing level of measurement error, which was evident in its lower coverage probabilities. (2017) furthered the work of McCaffrey et al., (2015) in causal inference, by investigating the use of SIMEX in estimating the correct average treatment effect (Δ), when a covariate is measured with a slightly different measurement error structure, called the mean reverting measurement error, under the doubly robust estimation assumption in the models mentioned in the previous paragraph.

results.title: [PDF] Correcting for measurement error
results.content: Ton de Waal Summer school 2023 Correcting for measurement error • Based on work by former PhD student Laura Boeschoten Correcting for measurement error • We have several data sources that can be linked on unit level • Same target variable is measured (with measurement error) in those data sources • We aim to correct for measurement error • We also aim to estimate accuracy of the corrected data The situation • Over-imputation  In over-imputation, imputation model is estimated and all values of target variable are imputed, including observed values • Structural equation modelling (SEM)  SEM can be used to model each observed value as an imperfect measure of underlying latent (unobserved) variable • Latent class modelling • Latent class modelling can be used to model each observed value of categorical variable as an imperfect measure of underlying latent (unobserved) variable with the true values Possible methods • Home-ownership: available in register and observed in survey • (Un)employment: employment/unemployment available in register and observed in Labour Force Survey Examples • Multiple Imputation  Uses bootstrap in background • Latent Class modelling Two elements in Laura’s approach (MILC) • Latent class analysis  Statistical modelling technique with many applications  In this workshop: focus on the use of latent class analysis for correcting for measurement errors in observed data  Requires multiple measurements for each unit Model introduction Latent class analysis (LCA) • Measure something that cannot be measured
